{{smaller|'''Food yolk.''' See ''food-yolk'', ''meroblastic'', and ''tropholecithus''. —'''Formative yolk,''' germinal yolk, which enters into the formation of the embryo, as distinguished from the food-yolk, which does not undergo segmentation; morpholecithus; vitellus germinativus. See ''holoblastic''.—'''Glycerite of yolk of egg,''' a mixture of yolk of egg (45 parts) with glycerin (55 parts), used as a vehicle for medicinal oils and resins.}}

'''yolk<sup>2</sup>''', ''v.'' See ''yoke<sup>2</sup>''. ''Halliwell.''

'''yolk-bag''' (yōk′bag), ''n.'' Same as ''yolk-sac''.

'''yolk-cleavage''' (yōk′klē″vạ̄j), ''n.'' In ''embryol.'', segmentation of the vitellus (which see, under ''segmentation''). See cut under ''gastrulation''.

'''yolk-duct''' (yōk′dukt), ''n.'' In ''embryol.'', the ductus vitellinus, or vitelline duct, which conducts from the cavity of the umbilical vesicle to that of the intestine through a constriction, at and near the navel, of the original globular cavity of the yolk-sac. See cut under ''embryo''.

'''yolked''' (yōkt), ''a.'' [< ''yolk'' + ''-ed<sup>2</sup>''.] Furnished with a yolk or vitellus: frequently used in composition: as, a double-''yolked'' egg.
{{smaller block|The effect of the loss of a large food-yolk . . . was shown to resemble a similar loss of food-yolk in the eggs of Micrometrus as compared with other large-''yolked'' oviparous fish eggs.
{{right|''Amer. Nat.'', XXIII. 923.}}}}

'''yolk-gland''' (yōk′gland), ''n.'' Same as ''vitellarium''.

'''yolk-sac''' (yōk′sak), ''n.'' The umbilical vesicle (which see, under ''vesicle''). Also called ''yolk-bag''. See cuts under ''embryo'' and ''uterus''.
{{smaller block|While the yolk in the latter is minute as compared with that of the former, the ''yolksack'' is just as large.
{{right|''Amer. Nat.'', XXIII. 926.}}}}

{{smaller block|Met me walking on ''yonder'' way.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Edward Gray.}}}}

'''yong†''', '''yonghede†''', '''yongth†''', etc. Obsolete forms of ''young'', etc.

'''yonker†''', ''n.'' An obsolete spelling of ''younker''.

'''yook''' (yök), ''v.'' and ''n.'' Same as ''yuck''.

'''yoop''' (yöp), ''n.'' [Imitative; cf. ''whoop''<sup>1</sup>, ''cloop'', etc.] A word imitative of a hiccuping or sobbing sound. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|There was such a scuffling, and hugging, and kissing, and crying, with the hysterical ''yoops'' of Miss Swartz, . . . as no pen can depict.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Vanity Fair.}}}}

'''yopon''' (yō′pọn), ''n.'' Same as ''yapon.''

'''yore'''<sup>1</sup> (yōr), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''yore'', ''ȝore'', < AS. ''geára'', of yore, formerly an adverbial gen. of time, lit. ‘of years,’ gen. pl. of ''geár'', year: see ''year''.] In time past; long ago; in old time: now used only in the phrase ''of yore'' — that is, of old time; long ago.
{{smaller block|<poem>A man may serven bet and more to pay
In half a yer, althow it were no more,
Than sum man doth that hath served ful ''yore''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 476.}}

Whan Adam had synnyd, thou seydest ''yore''
That he xulde deye and go to helle.
{{right|''Coventry Mysteries'', p. 107.}}

In Times ''of yore'' an ancient Baron liv’d.
{{right|''Prior'', Henry and Emma.}}</poem>
Instead of the great tree that used to shelter the quiet little Dutch inn ''of yore'', there now was reared a tall naked pole.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 58.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''yore<sup>2</sup>''' (yōr), ''a.'' Same as ''yare''<sup>1</sup>. ''Halliwell.''

'''Yoredale rocks.''' In ''Eng. geol.'', the upper portion of the Carboniferous limestone series. {{smaller|In this—as in the Pennine area—the massive limestone (the Thick, Scaur, or Main limestone) is succeeded by a series of flagstones, grits, shales, limestones, with a few seams of coal, the whole varying greatly in thickness in localities not far distant from each other. This series was named from Yoredale, in Yorkshire, where it has a development of from 500 to 1,500 feet. In its paleontological features it does not differ much from the Carboniferous limestone series generally. In the Yoredale rocks are the celebrated lead-mines of Alston Moor and others. Also called ''Yoredale group'' and ''Yoredale series.''}}

'''York-and-Lancaster rose.''' See ''rose''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Yorkish''' (yôr′kish), ''a.'' [< ''York'' (see def.) + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Pertaining to the city of York or to the county of York, in England.—'''2.''' Adhering to the house of York. See ''Yorkist.''
{{smaller block|<poem>But if thy ruby lip it spy,
As kiss it thou mayest deign,
With envy pale ’twill lose its dye,
And ''Yorkish'' turn again.</poem>
{{right|''The White Rose.''}}}}

'''Yorkist''' (yôr′kist), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ''York'' (see def.) + ''-ist.''] '''I.''' ''n.'' An adherent of the house of York, or a supporter of their claims to the crown, especially in the Wars of the Roses.
{{smaller block|The next Henry Percy, fourth earl, was, however, restored by Edward IV. and became a ''Yorkist.''
{{right|''Edinburgh Rev.'', CLXVIII. 379.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' In ''Eng. hist.'', pertaining to the dukes or the royal house of York. {{smaller|The Yorkist kings were Edward IV., Edward V., and Richard III. (1461–85), and their claims to the crown rested on their descent from Lionel, Duke of Clarence, and Edmund, Duke of York, respectively the third and fifth sons of Edward III. See ''Lancastrian'', and ''Wars of the Roses'' (under ''rose''<sup>1</sup>).}}
readings.c3s1:
¶
{{smaller block|The grand episode or tragedy of Perkin [Warbeck] . . . connects the ''Yorkist'' intrigues with the social discontents in a way more striking than any of the previous outbursts.
{{right|''Stubbs'', Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 348.}}}}

'''York pitch.''' See ''pitch of a plane'', under ''pitch''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Yorkshire flannel.''' Flannel of superior quality, made of undyed wool.

'''Yorkshire pudding.''' A pudding made of batter without sweets of any kind, and baked under meat, so as to catch the drippings.

'''Yorkshire stone.''' Stone from the Millstone-grit series, extensively quarried in Yorkshire, England, for building and various other purposes.

'''Yorkshire terrier.''' See ''terrier''<sup>1</sup>.

'''yorling''' (yôr′ling), ''n.'' Same as ''yolling.'' See ''yowley.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Half a paddock, half a toad,
Half a yellow ''yorling.''</poem>
{{right|''Scotch Ballad.''}}}}

'''Yoshino lacquer.''' See ''lacquer.''

'''yostreger†''', ''n.'' Same as ''austringer.''
{{smaller block|On of y<sup>e</sup> ''yostregere'' unto . . . Henry the VIII.
{{right|''Epitaph'', quoted in N. and Q., 7th ser., VIII. 106.}}}}

'''yot''' (yot), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''yotted'', ppr. ''yotting.'' [Prob. a var. of ''yote'', melt, hence weld: see ''yote''.] To unite closely; fasten; rivet. [Prov. Eng.]

'''yote''' (yōt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''yoted'', ppr. ''yoting.'' [< ME. ''yoten'', var. of ''yeten'', ''ȝeten'', ''ȝeoten'', < AS. ''geótan'', pour: see ''yet''<sup>2</sup>.] To pour water on; steep. [Obsolete or provincial.]
{{smaller block|<poem>My fowls, which well enough
I, as before, found feeding at their trough
Their ''yoted'' wheat.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Odyssey, xix. 760.}}}}

¶
'''ou''', ''pron.'' See ''ye''<sup>1</sup>.

'''ouk''' (youk), ''v. i.'' See ''yuck.''

'''oul†''', ''v. i.'' See ''yowl.''

'''ouling†''', ''n.'' A spelling of ''yowling.''

'''oung''' (yung), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''yong''; < ME. ''yong, yung, ʒung, ʒong, ʒing,'' < AS. ''geong, giung, iung'' (in compar. also ''ging-, gyng-, geng-'') = OFries. ''jung, jong'' = OS. ''jung'' = D. ''jong'' = MLG. ''junk,'' LG. ''jung'' = OHG. MHG. ''junc,'' G. ''jung'' = Icel. ''jungr, ungr'' = Sw. Dan. ''ung'' = Goth. ''juggs'' (compar. ''juhiza''?); Teut. *''yūnga,'' contr. of *''yuwanga'' or *''yuwanha'' = W. ''ieuangc'' = L. ''juvencus'' = Skt. ''yuvaça,'' young; an extension or derivative, with adj. suffix (L. ''-cu-s''), of a simpler form seen in L. ''juvenis'' = OBulg. ''junŭ'' = Russ. ''iunuiĭ,'' etc., = Lith. ''jaunus'' = Lett. ''jauns'' = Skt. ''yuvan,'' young; cf. Skt. ''yavishtha,'' youngest. From E. ''young'' is ult. E. ''youth.'' From the L. word are ult. E. ''juvenile, juvenal, juvenescent, rejuvenate,'' etc.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Being in the first or early stage of life; not long born; not yet arrived at maturity or full age; not old: said of animals: as, a ''young'' child; a ''young'' man; a ''young'' horse.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thow art ''ʒonge'' and ʒepe, and hast ʒeres ynowe
Forto lyue longe and ladyes to louye.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xi. 17.}}
<poem>Let the ''young'' lambs bound
As to the tabor’s sound!</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth,'' Ode, Immortality.}}}}
'''2.''' Being in the first or early stage of growth: as, a ''young'' plant; a ''young'' tree.
{{smaller block|He cropped off the top of his ''young'' twigs.
{{right|Ezek. xvii. 4.}}}}
readings.c3s3:
<poem>{{smaller block|I wish’d myself the fair ''young'' beech
That here beside me stands.}}</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Talking Oak.}}}}

'''3.''' Being in the first or early part of existence generally; not yet far advanced, of long duration, or of full development; recent; newly come to pass or to be.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Rom.'' Is the day so ''young?''
''Ben.'' But new struck nine.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 1. 166.}}
<poem>Th’ impatient fervor . . . threat’ning death
To his ''young'' hopes.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iii. 504.}}}}

'''4.''' Having the appearance and freshness or vigor of youth; youthful in look or feeling; fresh; vigorous.
{{smaller block|Thei that duellen there and drynken often of that Welle, thei nevere han Sekenesse, and thei semen alle weys ''zonge.''
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 169.}}
He is only seven-and-thirty, very ''young'' for his age, and the most affectionate of creatures.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Lovel the Widower, vi.}}}}

'''5.''' Having little experience; ignorant; raw; green.
{{smaller block|We are yet but ''young'' in deed.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 4. 144.}}
<poem>How for to sell he knew not well,
For a butcher he was but ''young.''</poem>
{{right|''Robin Hood and the Butcher'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 34).}}}}

'''6.''' Pertaining or relating to youth; spent or passed during youth; youthful: as, in his ''younger'' days he was very hot-headed.

Stone from the Millstone-grit series, extensively quarried in Yorkshire, England, for building and various other purposes. '''Yorkshire terrier.''' See ''terrier''1. '''yorling''' (yôr′ling), ''n.'' From E. ''young'' is ult. E. ''youth.'' From the L. word are ult. E. ''juvenile, juvenal, juvenescent, rejuvenate,'' etc.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Being in the first or early stage of life; not long born; not yet arrived at maturity or full age; not old: said of animals: as, a ''young'' child; a ''young'' man; a ''young'' horse. {{smaller block|Thow art ''ʒonge'' and ʒepe, and hast ʒeres ynowe Forto lyue longe and ladyes to louye. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xi. 17.}}}} {{smaller block|Let the ''young'' lambs bound As to the tabor’s sound! {{right|''Wordsworth,'' Ode, Immortality.}}}} '''2.''' Being in the first or early stage of growth: as, a ''young'' plant; a ''young'' tree. {{smaller block|He cropped off the top of his ''young'' twigs. {{right|Ezek. xvii. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|I wish’d myself the fair ''young'' beech That here beside me stands.}} {{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Talking Oak.}}}} '''3.''' Being in the first or early part of existence generally; not yet far advanced, of long duration, or of full development; recent; newly come to pass or to be. {{smaller block|''Rom.'' Is the day so ''young?'' ''Ben.'' But new struck nine. {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., i. 1. 166.}}}} {{smaller block|Th’ impatient fervor . . . threat’ning death To his ''young'' hopes. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, iii. 504.}}}} '''4.''' Having the appearance and freshness or vigor of youth; youthful in look or feeling; fresh; vigorous. {{smaller block|Thei that duellen there and drynken often of that Welle, thei nevere han Sekenesse, and thei semen alle weys ''zonge.'' {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 169.}}}} {{smaller block|He is only seven-and-thirty, very ''young'' for his age, and the most affectionate of creatures. {{right|''Thackeray'', Lovel the Widower, vi.}}}} '''5.''' Having little experience; ignorant; raw; green. {{smaller block|We are yet but ''young'' in deed. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iii. 4. 144.}}}} {{smaller block|How for to sell he knew not well, For a butcher he was but ''young.'' {{right|''Robin Hood and the Butcher'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 34).}}}} '''6.''' Pertaining or relating to youth; spent or passed during youth; youthful: as, in his ''younger'' days he was very hot-headed.
